topic: Attribution isn’t incrementality: ROAS measures credit, not lift
selectedWhy: Recent posts covered pricing mechanics (returns as insurance, EMI as pricing interface), customer operations (cancellation as research), AI operating models, and retail discovery (catalog eligibility). This cycle shifts to growth measurement — a high-stakes, under-discussed mechanism where teams confuse attribution certainty with causal truth. The non-obvious tension: dashboards with decimals can still fund the wrong growth because they reward credit assignment (where demand landed) rather than incrementality (what spend caused).
journalTitle: Attribution Isn’t Incrementality: ROAS Measures Credit, Not Lift
linkedinDraft:
Attribution doesn’t tell you what worked.

It tells you who got the credit.

This is why a team can have “great ROAS” and still not be growing.

Attribution is answering a different question than the one leaders think they’re asking.

ROAS dashboards are credit-allocation systems built from observed paths. They’re useful for optimizing inside a channel — but they’re not a reliable measure of what your spend *caused*. Incrementality is a counterfactual question (“what would have happened without this campaign?”), which is why lift tests (holdouts, geo splits, etc.) are the right tool when you’re deciding where the next chunk of budget should go.

A few practical implications:

- Separate two decisions: optimization within a channel vs allocation across channels.
- Use platform ROAS tactically: iterate creative/audiences; don’t treat it as causal truth.
- Anchor on blended outcomes: blended CAC/payback + new customer rate are harder to game.
- Run periodic lift tests: one high-confidence holdout per quarter beats weekly dashboard debates.
- Watch for the trap: channels that harvest existing intent can look “efficient” while starving long-term demand creation.

Full version here:
https://mohitsaikrishna.in/journal/attribution-is-not-incrementality?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=attribution_incrementality

When you last moved budget, what evidence actually changed your mind: a platform ROAS number, a blended business metric, or a lift test?

journalPreview:
Attribution is a confidence trap. It feels precise because the dashboard has decimals.

The mismatch: attribution mostly tells you where demand landed; incrementality asks what spend caused. If you don’t separate the two, you’ll keep funding intent-harvesting channels and starving demand creation.

Playbook: anchor on a few blended truth metrics, use attribution tactically within channels, and run periodic lift tests for budget allocation.
